voiceInstructions: Warm, engaging female teacher with a natural General American English accent. Relaxed, welcoming and lightly playful, with a gentle smile and conversational rhythm. Keep scientific terms precise and avoid an announcer cadence. Slow down for equations, numbers and conversions. Give brief natural thinking pauses after questions. Do not add words or laughter absent from the script.
title: Centre of mass and rotational applications

sources.title: OpenStax: Moments of inertia and axis theorems

chapters.title: Find the point that represents the whole system
chapters.formula: r_CM = sum(m_i r_i) / M; F_external = M a_CM
points: Find the point that represents the whole system
chapters.script: Welcome back. In this class we will work through mass-weighted positions, axis theorems, angular momentum, beam equilibrium and rolling down an incline. Imagine two small masses joined by a light connector. Their centre of mass is a mass-weighted position, not necessarily the midpoint. Put 2 kg at x equals 0 and 3 kg at x equals 4 m. Multiply each position by its mass, add, then divide by total mass: (2 times 0 plus 3 times 4)/5 equals 2.4 m. The answer lies nearer the heavier mass. For positive masses on a line it must lie between the extreme positions; that is a useful check before trusting your arithmetic. Use the same weighted average separately for x, y and z components. A uniform straight rod has its centre of mass at its midpoint, but a nonuniform rod may not. For a continuous body, replace the particle sum by an integral over mass. Symmetry is often quicker: a uniform ring has its centre of mass at its geometric centre even though there is no material there. For a fixed-mass system, the net external force equals total mass times centre-of-mass acceleration. Internal forces can rearrange the particles but cannot by themselves change the total momentum. On a horizontal frictionless surface, a person walking along a movable platform shifts the platform oppositely while their combined horizontal centre of mass stays fixed if initially at rest. Always include both person and platform in that system.

chapters.title: An inertia value belongs to a specific axis
chapters.formula: I_parallel = I_CM + Md^2; planar I_z = I_x + I_y; k_g = sqrt(I/M)
points: An inertia value belongs to a specific axis
chapters.script: Moment of inertia sums mass times squared perpendicular distance from the chosen axis. For standard uniform bodies, identify the axis before choosing a formula. A thin ring about its central perpendicular axis has I equals MR squared; a uniform disk has I equals MR squared/2. A uniform solid sphere about a diameter has 2MR squared/5, while a thin spherical shell has 2MR squared/3. A uniform thin rod has ML squared/12 about a perpendicular midpoint axis. These shapes and axes are part of each formula. The parallel-axis theorem moves from an axis through the centre of mass to a parallel axis a distance d away: I equals the centre of mass moment of inertia plus Md squared. For a 3 kg uniform rod of length 2 m, midpoint inertia is 1 kilogram metre squared. Move to a perpendicular axis through its end: d equals 1 m, so the end axis moment of inertia equals 1 plus 3 equals 4 kilogram metre squared. Do not use the distance between arbitrary nonparallel axes. Starting from two off-centre axes also requires knowing their distances from the centre-of-mass axis, not blindly adding Md squared between them. For a thin planar lamina, the perpendicular-axis theorem states I z equals I x plus I y for two perpendicular in-plane axes intersecting at the point where the normal z axis passes. It does not apply to an arbitrary three-dimensional body. A uniform disk has equal diameter-axis inertias by symmetry, so each is MR squared/4. Radius of gyration is a length defined by I equals Mradius of gyration squared. It locates an equivalent inertia distance, not necessarily a physical ring of material.

chapters.title: Angular momentum needs a chosen reference
chapters.formula: L = r cross p; tau_external = dL/dt; fixed symmetry axis: L_axis = I omega
points: Angular momentum needs a chosen reference
chapters.script: For a particle, angular momentum about a point is r cross p. Its magnitude is mvr sin(theta), where theta is the angle between position and velocity. The perpendicular distance from the reference point to the particle's straight-line path is often easier: magnitude equals mv times that distance. A 2 kg particle moving at 3 metres per second on a straight path 0.5 m from the origin has angular momentum magnitude 3 kilogram metre squared per second, even though it is not moving in a circle. About a fixed point in an inertial frame, the net external torque equals the rate of change of total angular momentum. If that torque vanishes, angular momentum is conserved. For rotation about a fixed principal or symmetry axis, the axial component is I omega. Do not assume the vector angular momentum is parallel to angular velocity for every possible axis of a three-dimensional body. An isolated rotating system reduces its axial moment of inertia from 4 to 2 kilogram metre squared, starting at 3 radians per second, with negligible external torque about that axis. Initial angular momentum is 12 kilogram metre squared per second. The final angular speed is 6 radians per second. Does its rotational kinetic energy stay unchanged? Pause and compare. It rises from 18 to 36 J. Internal work during the rearrangement supplies the increase. Conservation of angular momentum does not automatically conserve rotational kinetic energy.

chapters.title: A stationary beam must satisfy two balances
chapters.formula: Static equilibrium: sum F = 0 and sum tau = 0
points: A stationary beam must satisfy two balances
chapters.script: A rigid body in static equilibrium needs both zero net external force and zero net external torque. Balanced forces alone do not prevent turning. Two equal opposite parallel forces on different lines of action form a couple: net force is zero but their torques can add. Choose a torque reference that removes an unknown reaction, then still check the force equation. Consider a horizontal uniform 4 m beam of mass 2 kg supported vertically at both ends. A 6 kg load sits 1 m from the left end. Use g equals 10 metres per second squared and neglect support friction. The beam weight is 20 N at its midpoint; the load weight is 60 N at x equals 1 m. Call the upward reactions the left reaction and the right reaction. Vertical equilibrium gives their sum as 80 N. Take torques about the left support, positive anticlockwise. The left reaction has zero lever arm. The right reaction contributes 4the right reaction; the two downward weights contribute minus 20 times 2 and minus 60 times 1. Therefore 4the right reaction equals 100, giving the right reaction equals 25 N and the left reaction equals 55 N. The larger reaction is near the load. If a support can only push, a calculated negative reaction would invalidate the assumed contact; do not quietly accept a downward normal force.

chapters.title: Rolling shares energy between translation and rotation
chapters.formula: Pure rolling: a = g sin(theta)/(1 + I_CM/(MR^2)); v^2 = 2gh/(1 + I_CM/(MR^2))
points: Rolling shares energy between translation and rotation
chapters.script: Release a uniform solid cylinder from rest down a fixed rough incline. Assume pure rolling on a stationary surface, sufficient static friction, no deformation losses and no rolling resistance. The centre accelerates downhill while static friction points uphill and supplies torque about the centre. Translational force balance gives mg sin(theta) minus f equals ma. Torque gives fR equals the centre of mass moment of inertia alpha, and no slip gives a equals R alpha. Combining them yields a equals g sin(theta)/(1 plus the centre of mass moment of inertia divided by mass times radius squared). For a solid cylinder the centre of mass moment of inertia is mass times radius squared divided by two. At 30 degrees with g equals 10 metres per second squared, its acceleration is 10/3 metres per second squared, not 5 metres per second squared. Some gravitational energy goes into rotation, so the centre accelerates less than a frictionless sliding particle. In ideal pure rolling the instantaneous contact point is stationary relative to the fixed surface. Static friction therefore does no net work on the rigid body here, although it redistributes translational and rotational energy. This conclusion need not hold for a moving surface. The required friction is mg sin(theta)/3 for the cylinder, while N equals mg cos(theta). Hence the no-slip condition is the coefficient of static friction must be at least tan(theta)/3. Below that coefficient, the rolling assumption fails and sliding must be treated separately. After a vertical drop h, energy gives v squared equals 2gh/(1 plus the centre of mass moment of inertia divided by mass times radius squared). A solid cylinder dropping 0.30 m with g equals 10 reaches 2 metres per second. A ring has a different inertia and a different final speed. Compare models, not just masses.

quiz.question: Masses 2 kg and 3 kg lie at x = 0 and x = 4 m. Their centre of mass is:
quiz.explanation: The mass-weighted position is (2 x 0 + 3 x 4)/(2 + 3) = 2.4 m, nearer the heavier mass.

quiz.question: A uniform 3 kg, 2 m thin rod has a perpendicular axis through one end. Its moment of inertia is:
quiz.explanation: I_CM = ML^2/12 = 1. Shift by L/2 = 1 m to the parallel end axis: I = 1 + 3(1)^2 = 4 kg m^2.

quiz.question: With zero external axial torque, I changes from 4 to 2 kg m^2. Initial angular speed is 3 rad/s. Final angular speed is:
quiz.explanation: Conserved axial angular momentum gives 4 x 3 = 2 omega_final, so omega_final = 6 rad/s. Kinetic energy need not stay constant.

quiz.question: A uniform 4 m beam weighs 20 N; a 60 N load is 1 m from its left support. The upward right support reaction is:
quiz.explanation: Torque about the left support: 4R_right = 20 x 2 + 60 x 1 = 100. Hence R_right = 25 N; force balance gives R_left = 55 N.

quiz.question: A uniform solid cylinder rolls from rest without slipping through a vertical drop of 0.30 m. With g = 10, its final centre speed is:
quiz.explanation: Use v^2 = 2gh/(1 + I_CM/(MR^2)). For a solid cylinder the inertia ratio is 1/2, giving v^2 = 6/1.5 = 4 and v = 2 m/s.
